summary.en: A civil war in Japan in 1180–1185 between the Taira and Minamoto clans. The Minamoto won, and Minamoto no Yoritomo founded the shogunate in Kamakura. The war marked the beginning of the power of the warrior class, the samurai, in Japan.

text.en: The dates have been converted from the Japanese lunar calendar, and Wikidata gives them in the Julian calendar. The sources sometimes give different dates: the naval battle of Dan-no-ura is given as 25 April 1185 in Wikipedia and Wikidata, but as 24 March 1185 on the official page of the city of Shimonoseki.

intro.en: The Taira and Minamoto clans had long fought over influence at the imperial court. After the Heiji Rebellion of 1159 the Taira dominated, and in 1179 Taira no Kiyomori removed his rivals from all offices. In 1180 he put his two-year-old grandson Antoku on the throne. Prince Mochihito, who felt passed over, and Minamoto no Yorimasa then called the Minamoto clan and Buddhist monasteries to arms against the Taira.

members.en: Minamoto no Yoritomo, his half-brothers Yoshitsune and Noriyori, with the Miura, Takeda, Hōjō and Chiba clans. Yoritomo's cousin Minamoto no Yoshinaka fought against the Taira but in 1183 also turned against Yoritomo.
The Taira clan under Kiyomori and, after his death in 1181, his son Munemori, with the young emperor Antoku.

outcome.en: The Taira were finally defeated at Dan-no-ura in 1185, where the young emperor Antoku also died. The same year Yoritomo gained the right to appoint stewards and constables in all provinces, and in 1192 he was appointed shogun. Real power now lay with the warrior government in Kamakura, while the emperor in Kyoto had a ceremonial role until the Meiji Restoration more than 650 years later. The colours of the Taira and the Minamoto, red and white, became Japan's national colours.

casualties.en: The sources give no estimate of how many died in the war. From 1181 Japan was also struck by a famine that lasted into the following year.

summary.en: On 20 June 1180 the Taira forces catch up with Prince Mochihito and Minamoto no Yorimasa at the bridge over the Uji River. Yorimasa takes his own life in the Byōdō-in temple, and the prince is also killed. The battle is considered the start of the war.

On 2 June 1183 Minamoto no Yoshinaka holds a large Taira army in the Kurikara mountain pass until dark and then attacks it from several directions. The Taira suffer a heavy defeat and soon have to leave the capital, Kyoto. The battle turns the war in favour of the Minamoto.

On 20 March 1184 Minamoto no Yoshitsune and Noriyori attack the Taira fortified camp on the narrow coastal strip from two directions, Yoshitsune with a small cavalry force from the mountains to the north. Only about 3,000 Taira escape to Yashima.

On 22 March 1185 Yoshitsune lands on Shikoku and lights beacon fires behind the Taira camp at Yashima. The Taira expect an attack from the sea, believe that a large army is coming overland, and flee out to their ships, with Emperor Antoku and the imperial regalia.

On 25 April 1185 the fleets meet in the strait between Honshu and Kyushu. The tide favours first the Taira and then the Minamoto, and one of the Taira commanders goes over to the enemy in the middle of the battle. The Taira are defeated, and the young emperor Antoku dies together with many of the clan's leaders. The war is over.

caption.en: The naval battle of Dan-no-ura, two of eight panels in the painting about Emperor Antoku, on gold paper. Attributed to Tosa Mitsunobu, before about 1525. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Kublai Khan, who ruled over the Mongols' Yuan Empire in China, tried twice, in 1274 and 1281, to conquer Japan with fleets from Korea and China. Both invasions failed. The second fleet was destroyed by a typhoon that the Japanese called kamikaze, “divine wind”.

text.en: The dates have been converted from the lunar calendar, and Wikidata gives them in the Julian calendar. The sources sometimes give different days for the same event, so several events in the war are given only by month.

intro.en: After several Mongol invasions, Korea, the kingdom of Goryeo, became a vassal state of the Mongols. Between 1266 and 1273 Kublai Khan sent six embassies to Japan demanding submission, but Japan, which was ruled by regents from the Hōjō clan in the Kamakura shogunate, did not reply. In 1274 he sent an invasion fleet from Korea.

members.en: The Kamakura shogunate under the regent Hōjō Tokimune, with warriors from clans such as Shōni, Ōtomo, Kikuchi, Shimazu and Sō.

Kublai Khan's Yuan Empire with Mongol, Han Chinese and Jurchen soldiers, and the vassal state Goryeo in Korea, which had to build the ships and provide soldiers and sailors. In 1281 a fleet also came from southern China.

outcome.en: Japan kept its independence, and the invasions set a limit to Mongol expansion. The Yuan Empire lost most of its naval power, and Korea, which had built the ships, was weakened. Because the defensive war yielded no new land, the shogunate could not reward its warriors, and its prestige declined. The word kamikaze was later taken up again during the Second World War.

casualties.en: The figures are uncertain. According to Stephen Turnbull, about 13,500 of the roughly 30,000 in the first invasion did not return, and in the second more than 120,000 died. Chinese and Mongol sources state that 60–90 per cent were lost, and a Korean source that 7,592 of 26,989 Koreans did not come home. The historians Thomas Conlan and Morris Rossabi hold that the fleets were considerably smaller than the chronicles say. How many Japanese died is unknown.

summary.en: In November 1274 the invasion fleet, which has sailed from Korea, lands on the island of Tsushima. The island's small defence force under Sō Sukekuni is defeated, and Sukekuni is killed. The fleet continues to the island of Iki and then towards Kyushu.

The Yuan army lands in Hakata Bay and drives the Japanese warriors away from the beach with close ranks, explosive charges and arrows, and the town of Hakata burns. But the army returns to the ships, and in the morning the fleet has vanished. A storm destroys many ships, and the invasion is called off.

text.en: Wikipedia's main article says that the fleet landed on 19 November and that the battle took place the following day, while the article on the battle gives 4–19 November. Wikidata gives November 1274. The month and the place agree.

summary.en: In June 1281 the eastern fleet from Korea attacks the islands of Tsushima and Iki and tries to land in Hakata Bay, but a stone wall that the Japanese had built after the previous invasion stops it. The Japanese attack the ships with small boats at night. When the southern fleet from China has joined, the fighting ends in a stalemate.

On 15 August 1281 a great typhoon strikes the Yuan fleet, which is lying at anchor. Many ships go down, including in Imari Bay, and thousands of soldiers are stranded. The Japanese attack the stranded men and take tens of thousands prisoner, and the invasion is over. The storm was called kamikaze, “divine wind”.

title.en: Only one source for the place

text.en: Wikidata gives August 1281, which agrees, but no place. The place comes only from Wikipedia.

caption.en: The Mongol fleet is destroyed in a typhoon. Ink and watercolour on paper by Kikuchi Yōsai, 1847, in the Tokyo National Museum. An artist's image more than 500 years later. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: During the 13th century the Mongols, first under Genghis Khan and then under his descendants, conquered large parts of Asia and Eastern Europe. The campaigns created the largest contiguous empire in history. Shown here is the period from the first major campaign in 1209 to the fall of the Song dynasty in 1279.

text.en: The sources give different spans. Wikipedia writes that the conquests went on during the 13th and 14th centuries, and Wikidata gives 1206–1337. Shown here is 1209–1279: from the first major campaign, against Western Xia in April 1209, to the Battle of Yamen on 19 March 1279, when the Song dynasty fell and the Mongols ruled all of China. The empire began to split into khanates from 1260, and the later wars are not included.

intro.en: Temüjin united the tribes on the Mongolian plateau and became ruler of a new empire, the Mongol Empire, with the title Genghis Khan (1206). He wanted to plunder richer neighbours, make them tribute-paying vassals and avenge old wrongs, and attacked Western Xia in 1209 and the Jin dynasty in northern China in 1211. According to the historian Christopher Atwood, Genghis Khan saw the war as a personal revenge against rulers who had defied him. The idea of conquering the whole world grew gradually and was official ideology in the 1240s.

members.en: The Mongols under Genghis Khan and his successors, with troops from subjugated and allied countries, for example Western Xia after 1210 and Armenia and Georgia in the Middle East. After 1260 the Ilkhanate in Persia and the Yuan dynasty in China carried on the wars.

Among others Western Xia, the Jin dynasty and the Song dynasty in China, the Khwarazmian Empire in Central Asia and Persia, the principalities of Kievan Rus' and the Cumans, the Kingdom of Hungary, the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad and the Mamluks in Egypt.

outcome.en: The Mongol Empire became the largest contiguous empire in history. In 1260 it covered a large part of Eurasia and at its greatest extent stretched from the Pacific Ocean to Central Europe. From 1260 the empire split into khanates. The Mamluk victory at Ain Jalut in 1260 stopped the advance in the Middle East, and after the Battle of Yamen in 1279 the Mongols ruled all of China under the Yuan dynasty.

casualties.en: Very uncertain. Estimates for the Mongol conquests as a whole range from about 30 million dead (R. J. Rummel) to as many as 80 million. The Iranian plateau may have lost up to three quarters of its population, perhaps 10–15 million people, through violence, famine and disease. China's population appears to have halved, but scholars disagree about how much is due to the war, to shortcomings in the census or to the plague. The figures are estimates and are given as ranges.

summary.en: In 1209 Genghis Khan begins his first major campaign, against the Tangut empire of Western Xia in north-western China. After a siege of the capital lasting almost a year, the emperor sues for peace in January 1210, and Western Xia becomes a vassal of the Mongols.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the Mongol conquests says the attack began in April 1209, while the article on Yinchuan writes autumn 1209. Wikidata has only the whole conquest of Western Xia (1205–1227), not this campaign.

summary.en: After a long blockade and starvation, the Jin dynasty's capital Zhongdu, present-day Beijing, surrenders to the Mongols in 1215. The Jin court had already moved south to Kaifeng. The loss is a decisive blow to the power of the Jin dynasty in northern China.

text.en: Wikipedia gives both 31 May and June 1215 for the capitulation, and Wikidata gives 1 June 1215. The year and the place agree.

summary.en: In February 1220, during the campaign against the Khwarazmian Empire (1219–1221), a Mongol army under Genghis Khan crosses the Kyzylkum Desert and takes the trade and cultural city of Bukhara by surprise. The city surrenders after three days and the citadel falls within two weeks.
On 31 May 1223 a Mongol force under Jebe and Subutai defeats a united army from several principalities of Kievan Rus' and the Cumans. The Mongols then turn back east to Genghis Khan.

On 11 April 1241 the Mongols under Batu crush King Béla IV's Hungarian army. The victory cost the Mongols dearly, which contributed to the campaign in Europe being broken off. The following year the Mongols withdrew from Central Europe.

A Mongol army under Hülegü attacks Baghdad at the end of January 1258. The caliph al-Musta'sim surrenders the city on 10 February, the city is sacked and the caliph is executed. How many died is unknown; Hülegü himself stated about 200,000. The fall has traditionally been seen as the end of the Islamic Golden Age, but its consequences are debated.

caption.en: The Mongols besiege Baghdad in 1258. Miniature in a manuscript of Rashid al-Din's world history, painted about 1430–1434, in the Bibliothèque nationale de France. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 3 September 1260 the Mamluks from Egypt under Qutuz defeat a Mongol army under Kitbuqa. It is the first time the Mongol advance is stopped for good, and they withdraw from the Levant.

On 19 March 1279 the fleet of the Yuan dynasty defeats the last forces of the Song dynasty in a naval battle at Yamen. The Song dynasty's last emperor, the child Zhao Bing, drowns. The battle ends the Mongol conquest of the Song Empire, and the Yuan then rule all of China.

text.en: Wikipedia and Wikidata give the same date, 19 March 1279. Wikidata gives it in the Gregorian calendar for the battle but in the Julian calendar as the end date of the conquest of the Song Empire. We show the date as the sources write it.

summary.en: The Ming dynasty is founded in Nanjing on 23 January 1368 and rules China until 1644. The capital is formally moved to Beijing in 1420.

summary.en: Over a little more than a hundred years, 622–750, the Islamic state grew from Medina into an empire stretching from Sindh in present-day Pakistan to the Iberian Peninsula, an estimated 13 million square kilometres. The conquests are also called the early Muslim or Islamic conquests.

intro.en: In 622 Muhammad founded the first Islamic state in Medina, and in 630 his followers took Mecca. After his death in 632 the first caliph, Abu Bakr, united the Arabian Peninsula. The two great powers to the north, the Byzantine Empire and the Persian Sasanian Empire, were according to most historians exhausted by decades of war against each other and by outbreaks of plague, and the Sasanians had also had a civil war in 628–632. The armies from Arabia first advanced towards Syria and Iraq and then onwards in all directions under the Rashidun caliphs and the Umayyad dynasty.

members.en: The first Islamic state in Medina, the Rashidun Caliphate (632–661) and the Umayyad Caliphate (661–750).

In the Middle East and North Africa: the Sasanian Empire, the Byzantine Empire, the Kingdom of Makuria and the Khazars. In Central Asia, among others the Western Turkic Khaganate, the Türgesh and the Tang dynasty. In South Asia the Chach dynasty and the Karkota dynasty. In Europe the Visigothic Kingdom, the Kingdom of Asturias and the Franks.

outcome.en: The Sasanian Empire fell, and the Byzantine Empire kept only parts of Anatolia and South-Eastern Europe. The caliphate stretched from Sindh to Septimania in southern France. By the middle of the 8th century the conquests came to a halt: the armies had reached natural borders and strong states, and the rulers devoted themselves more to governing the empire. In 750 the Umayyads were overthrown by the Abbasids. The spread of Islam then went more slowly, through local dynasties, missionaries and merchants.

casualties.en: The sources give no estimate of how many died during the conquests as a whole. For individual battles there are figures that diverge, for example at Yarmouk: according to Arabic primary sources 70,000–120,000 died on the Byzantine side, while modern estimates say over 30,000; on the Muslim side about 9,000 dead are given (Akram).

summary.en: Over six days in August 636 the armies of the Rashidun Caliphate defeat a large Byzantine army that Emperor Heraclius had sent to retake Syria. The victory effectively ended Byzantine rule in Syria.

text.en: Wikipedia and Wikidata give the same coordinates, but Wikipedia marks them as doubtful. The point shows the area by the Yarmouk River, not an exact battlefield site.

caption.en: The Battle of Yarmouk in a small picture at the bottom of a page in a manuscript from about 1310–1325, by an unknown Catalan illustrator, in the Bibliothèque nationale de France. The armour is from the picture's own time, not from the 7th century. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In November 636 the Rashidun Caliphate defeats the army of the Sasanian Empire at al-Qadisiyya. The Persians were then unable to defend the capital Ctesiphon and withdrew from all of Mesopotamia. The Sasanian Empire was completely conquered in 651.

text.en: Wikipedia writes that it is generally accepted that the fighting began on 16 November 636 and lasted for three days. Wikidata gives the same date.

summary.en: The army of the Rashidun Caliphate under Abu Ubayda besieges Jerusalem from November 636. After six months the patriarch Sophronius agrees to surrender, but only before the caliph himself, and Umar travels to Jerusalem to receive the city. Jerusalem then remained under Muslim rule until the First Crusade in 1099.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the siege lasted from November 636 to April 637 and that Umar received the city in 637 or 638. Wikidata gives November 636 to April 637.

summary.en: An army under Amr ibn al-As enters Egypt in December 639 and takes the Babylon Fortress in 641. Under an armistice the last Byzantine troops left Alexandria in September 642, and on 29 September Amr marched into the city. The conquest ended seven hundred years of Roman rule in Egypt.
In 642 the Rashidun Caliphate defeats the army of the Sasanian king Yazdegerd III at Nahavand. It was the end of organised Sasanian resistance, and Yazdegerd fled east towards Merv.

text.en: Wikipedia and Wikidata agree on the year and that the battle took place at Nahavand. However, Wikidata's coordinates for the battle are the same as for al-Qadisiyya in Iraq, which is wrong. The point here is the town of Nahavand according to Wikidata.

summary.en: In July 711 the army of the Umayyad Caliphate, mainly Berbers and some Arabs under Tariq ibn Ziyad, defeats the Visigoths. King Roderic is killed, and the way opens towards the capital Toledo. The battle became the beginning of al-Andalus, Muslim Spain.

text.en: According to Wikipedia it is not known where the battle took place, only that it was by a body of water in southern Spain. Wikidata places it at the Guadalete River and gives the day as 19 July 711 (Julian calendar). The point is approximate.

summary.en: In October 732 Franks and Aquitanians under Charles Martel defeat an Umayyad army under the governor of al-Andalus, Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, who is killed. Details such as the size of the armies and the exact place are unclear. Many historians have seen the victory as important for halting the spread of Islam in Western Europe, but the revolts among the Berbers in North Africa and Spain may have mattered more.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the battle and Wikidata give 10 October 732. Wikipedia's article on the Arab conquests writes that the battle took place sometime between 18 and 25 October 732. Wikidata's coordinates lie at Tours, about 20 km north of the place that Wikipedia gives.

summary.en: On 25 January 750 the Abbasid army defeats the Umayyads at the Greater Zab River. It meant the end of the Umayyad Caliphate, and the Abbasid Caliphate took over and lasted until 1258. With the Abbasid revolution the time of the early conquests is usually considered over.

A series of campaigns launched by the papacy in 1095–1291 against Muslim rulers, to conquer and defend the Holy Land. The crusaders founded four states in the Levant, but the last strongholds on the mainland fell in 1291. In a wider sense, crusades against other enemies are also counted, for example in Spain and around the Baltic Sea.

text.en: Wikipedia and Wikidata both give 1095–1291. Here the war begins with the Council of Clermont in November 1095 and ends with the fall of Acre on 18 May 1291.

intro.en: After the Seljuks defeated the Byzantine Empire at Manzikert in 1071, Turkomans had moved into Anatolia, and Byzantine rule there collapsed. In March 1095 Emperor Alexios I Komnenos asked Pope Urban II for military help. The Seljuk Empire was then split by civil war. In November 1095 Urban II, at the Council of Clermont, urged Christians to retake Jerusalem from the Muslims, and promised spiritual reward to those who joined.

members.en: Armies from Catholic Europe, called together by the papacy, and the crusader states in the Levant: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the Principality of Antioch and the counties of Tripoli and Edessa. They also included the military orders, and Italian trading cities such as Venice, Pisa and Genoa helped with ships.
Various realms in different periods: Seljuk princes and the Fatimids in Egypt during the First Crusade, then the Zengids, the Ayyubids under Saladin and finally the Mamluks in Egypt and Syria.

outcome.en: The First Crusade conquered Jerusalem in 1099, but after the Battle of Hattin in 1187 Saladin retook the city and most of the crusader states. The Third Crusade saved some of them, and the Fourth ended with the crusaders sacking the Christian city of Constantinople in 1204. The Mamluks united Egypt and Syria and in 1291 took the crusaders' last strongholds on the mainland, among them Acre.

casualties.en: The sources give no estimate of how many died during all the crusades. For individual events there are figures: when the crusaders took Jerusalem in 1099, an estimated 3,000–10,000 Muslims and Jews were killed, at Edessa in 1144 5,000–6,000 civilians were killed, and during the siege of Acre in 1189–1191 about 19,000 died on the crusader side according to the historian Hosler, while another estimate (HistoryNet) speaks of up to 100,000 dead and wounded.

summary.en: The Council of Clermont takes place on 17–27 November 1095. On the last day Pope Urban II delivers the speech that calls for the First Crusade. The council was otherwise mostly about reforms in the Church and local matters.

The First Crusade besieges Jerusalem, which was then ruled by the Fatimids in Egypt, from 7 June 1099. With siege towers the crusaders enter the city on 15 July and massacre thousands of Muslims and Jews. Shortly afterwards the Kingdom of Jerusalem is founded.

caption.en: The crusaders take Jerusalem in 1099. Late medieval book illumination, probably from Sébastien Mamerot's Les Passages d'oultre mer; artist and year are unknown. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Zengi, ruler of Mosul and Aleppo, takes Edessa, capital of the first crusader state. The loss became the reason for the Second Crusade, which failed in 1148.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the siege and Wikidata state that it lasted from 28 November to 24 December 1144. Wikipedia's article on the crusades writes that the city fell on 26 December 1144.

summary.en: On 3–4 July 1187 the Ayyubid sultan Saladin defeats the combined army of the crusader states. Almost the entire army was killed or taken prisoner. Saladin then took Jerusalem and most of the crusader cities, which led to the Third Crusade.

From August 1189 to July 1191 the crusaders besiege Acre, in what became the Third Crusade. Both sides received supplies by sea. The crusaders took the city, a severe setback for Saladin, and Acre became the capital of the Kingdom of Jerusalem.

The Fourth Crusade, which was first meant to go against Egypt, turns against the Byzantine Empire. In April 1204 the crusaders sack Constantinople and found the Latin Empire. The Byzantines retook the city in 1261, but the empire never regained its former strength.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 12–15 April 1204. Wikidata gives 13 April 1204, and the siege 8–13 April according to the Julian calendar.

summary.en: The Mamluk Sultanate in Egypt besieges Acre from 4 April 1291 and takes the city on 18 May. The crusaders thereby lost their last major stronghold in the Kingdom of Jerusalem, and no more crusades to the Levant came about. The crusading movement did, however, continue in other forms.

At the end of September or beginning of October 207, in the last years of the Han dynasty, the warlord Cao Cao defeats the nomadic Wuhuan and their allies Yuan Shang and Yuan Xi north of the empire's border. The power of the Wuhuan is broken, and northern China is united under Cao Cao shortly before the time of the Three Kingdoms.

text.en: The Historical Conflict Event Dataset places the battle in present-day Ningxia, far to the west. Wikipedia states that it took place near present-day Lingyuan in Liaoning, and we follow Wikipedia. Wikidata gives the year 207 but no place, so the place could not be compared with a second source.

summary.en: Shortly after Ctesiphon has fallen, the Sasanian Empire gathers its remaining armies at Jalula, where the roads towards Iraq, Khorasan and Azerbaijan meet. In April 637 an Arab army of about 12,000 men from the Rashidun Caliphate defeats the Persians there. The town is then besieged for seven months before it surrenders.
Around 1235 the Mandinka prince Sundiata Keita defeats King Sumanguru Kanté of Sosso at Kirina. The victory makes Sundiata's new Mali Empire the leading power in West Africa.

text.en: The Historical Conflict Event Dataset places the battle about 80 km north-east of the place that Wikipedia and Wikidata give. We follow Wikipedia and Wikidata, which agree with each other. The year, about 1235, is the same in all the sources.

summary.en: The Maya city of Caracol had been subordinate to Tikal, but in April 562 Caracol's king Yajaw Te' K'inich II defeats Tikal in a so-called star war, probably as an ally of Calakmul. Tikal's king appears to have been captured and sacrificed. Tikal is not sacked, but its power is broken, and the city enters a hiatus of over a hundred years without new monuments.

text.en: The information is based on inscriptions, above all the damaged Altar 21 at Caracol, which are interpreted by scholars. Wikipedia's articles on Caracol and Tikal both give the year 562, and the article on Tikal gives April. There is no Wikidata entry for the war.

summary.en: The king of Mali, Mansa Musa, reaches Cairo in July 1324 on his pilgrimage to Mecca. His retinue attracts attention with its size and wealth.

caption.en: Mansa Musa on his throne holding a gold nugget, as he was drawn on the Catalan Atlas in 1375, half a century after the journey. Map in pen and coloured inks on parchment, attributed to Abraham Cresques. Detail. Public domain.

summary.en: On 14 June 1325, 21-year-old Ibn Battuta leaves his hometown of Tangier to make the pilgrimage to Mecca. It is the start of journeys that last for many years.

caption.en: An imaginary drawing of Ibn Battuta from a book published in Egypt in 1961. No image of him from his own time is known, so the drawing does not show what he looked like. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Jesus is crucified in Jerusalem, probably in AD 30 or 33. The event is described in the Gospels and in other sources from antiquity, and almost all scholars regard it as historical.

caption.en: The crucified Christ as painted by Diego Velázquez around 1632, in the Prado Museum in Madrid. An artist's image 1,600 years later, not a depiction from the time of the event. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: According to Islam, Muhammad receives his first revelation in the Cave of Hira near Mecca, the beginning of what becomes the Quran. The exact date is disputed, but most Muslims reckon it to be the year 610.

caption.en: Jabal an-Nur near Mecca, where the Cave of Hira is located. Contemporary photograph by Wal N., 2007. The Prophet is not depicted. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

summary.en: Sikhism emerges in Punjab around the end of the 15th century, from the teachings of Guru Nanak. He lives 1469–1539 and is the first of the Sikh gurus.

caption.en: Guru Nanak in a mural in Gurdwara Baba Atal, 19th century, painted by Jaimal Singh Naqqash, among others. Photograph by Amritpal Singh Mann. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: At L'Anse aux Meadows on the northern tip of Newfoundland there are traces of a Norse settlement. Carbon-14 dating gives the years 990–1050, and tree rings in wood show that Norse people were there in the year 1021. It is the only securely confirmed Norse site in North America outside Greenland, and it may be connected with the Icelandic sagas' accounts of Leif Eriksson. The site was excavated in 1961–1968 by Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad and became a World Heritage Site in 1978.

caption.en: The foundation of the largest Norse house at L'Anse aux Meadows on Newfoundland, photographed in 2010. Contemporary photo. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: Polynesians from eastern Polynesia become the first people in New Zealand, the last stop as the Polynesians settle ever further east across the Pacific. Over time they develop a culture of their own, the one known today as Māori. When they arrived is uncertain, but research points to the period between about 1250 and 1350.

text.en: Wikipedia gives both the years 1320–1350, based on the oldest traces of people, and the years 1250–1300, based on mitochondrial DNA.

caption.en: Early Māori objects from the Wairau Bar site, in Canterbury Museum in Christchurch. Contemporary museum photo from 2016. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Great Zimbabwe is a city of stone built by the ancestors of the Shona people. The major building begins in the 11th century, and from the 13th century the city is the capital of the Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe. Gold and ivory are carried via the Swahili cities, Sofala among them, out into the Indian Ocean trade, and glass beads and porcelain from China and Persia come back. The city is abandoned in the 16th or 17th century. Today it is a World Heritage Site.

caption.en: The Great Enclosure in the ruins of Great Zimbabwe, photographed in 1997. Contemporary photo. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In 1271 the Venetian Marco Polo sets out for Asia with his father Niccolò and his uncle Maffeo. About three and a half years later they reach Kublai Khan's palace in Shangdu. Marco travels around China and lives in the khan's realm for 17 years. In 1295 he returns home to Venice. As a prisoner in Genoa he tells Rustichello da Pisa about his travels, and Rustichello writes them down in 1298–1299. The account later inspired Christopher Columbus, among others.

caption.en: Marco Polo travelling. Miniature from a later manuscript of his travel account, not from the journey. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Between 1405 and 1433, Zheng He leads seven naval expeditions on behalf of the Chinese emperors Yongle and Xuande. The first fleet has 317 ships and almost 28,000 men. The voyages reach the Arabian Peninsula and the Horn of Africa, including Malindi on the East African coast, which sends a giraffe to China in 1414. The largest ships are described in a later novel as 127 metres long, but many scholars believe they were 60–75 metres.

caption.en: Sea chart of Zheng He's voyages from the Wubei zhi by Mao Yuanyi, woodcut in an edition from the 17th century. Later than the voyages. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 29 May 1453 the Ottoman Empire under Sultan Mehmed II conquers Constantinople, after a siege that began on 6 April. It marks the end of the Byzantine Empire and in practice the end of the Roman Empire. What happened to the last emperor, Constantine XI, is unknown. Mehmed makes the city the new capital of the Ottoman Empire.

caption.en: The siege of Constantinople in a French manuscript, Jean Chartier's chronicle of Charles VII, painted around 1460 and attributed to Philippe de Mazerolles. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 8 July 1497 Vasco da Gama leaves Lisbon with four ships. The fleet sails around the Cape of Good Hope and north along the East African coast to Malindi, where the sultan receives him well and he obtains a pilot. On 20 May 1498 he reaches Kozhikode in India. The voyage opens the first sea route between Europe and India.

caption.en: Vasco da Gama's arrival in Calicut in 1498, painted by Alfredo Roque Gameiro around 1900. Later image. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In AD 79 the volcano Vesuvius erupts and buries the Roman towns of Pompeii, Herculaneum, Oplontis and Stabiae. Pliny the Younger described the eruption in two letters, and his uncle Pliny the Elder died after sailing towards Stabiae to rescue a friend. How many died is unknown. Remains of over 1,500 people have been found in Pompeii and Herculaneum, and estimates range from 1,500–3,500 up to 16,000.

text.en: The date is disputed. The traditional day, 24 August, comes from a printed edition from 1508 of Pliny the Younger's letters. Several scholars believe the eruption took place in the autumn, and Wikidata gives 24 October or 23 November in the year 79.

caption.en: The Destruction of Pompeii and Herculaneum, painting by John Martin from 1822. Later image. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: King Ezana of Aksum, who reigns from the 320s to about 360, is converted to Christianity by his tutor Frumentius, who then becomes the leader of the Ethiopian church. On Aksum's coins the old symbol of a disc and crescent is replaced by a cross. According to tradition, Ezana had the first cathedral in Aksum built.

caption.en: Ezana's Stone in Aksum, with an inscription in Greek, Sabaean and Ge'ez about the king's conversion. Contemporary photo from 2011. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

summary.en: On 4 September 476 Odoacer, who leads the federate troops in Italy, takes Ravenna and deposes Romulus Augustulus, the last emperor of the West. Odoacer makes himself king of Italy without taking the imperial title and sends the imperial regalia to the emperor in the East. The year 476 has long been used as a convenient boundary for the end of the Western Roman Empire, but historians also point to other years.

caption.en: Gold coin (solidus) of Romulus Augustulus, the last Western Roman emperor, struck 475–476. Licence: CC0.

summary.en: On Christmas Day in the year 800 Charlemagne is crowned emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III in St Peter's in Rome. He becomes the first reigning emperor in the West since Romulus Augustulus was deposed in 476. The imperial title leads to conflict with the East in Constantinople.

caption.en: Charlemagne is crowned emperor in Rome. Miniature by Jean Fouquet in the Grandes Chroniques de France, around 1455–1460. Later image. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: During the 8th and 9th centuries many Maya cities in the southern lowlands decline, among them Palenque, Copán, Tikal and Calakmul, and they are abandoned shortly afterwards. The last monument in Tikal was erected in 869, and by the year 900 no more dated monuments are raised. Drought is today the most common explanation. The cities of the northern Yucatán, such as Chichén Itzá, Uxmal and Cobá, survive and flourish afterwards.

caption.en: The Great Plaza in Tikal, photographed in 2009. Contemporary photo. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

summary.en: Between 1113 and 1150 the Khmer Empire under King Suryavarman II builds the temple Angkor Wat in the capital Yaśodharapura. It is dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu and from the end of the 13th century gradually becomes a Theravada Buddhist temple, which it still is. It is the world's largest religious complex, and since 1863 an image of the temple has appeared on Cambodia's flag.

caption.en: Angkor Wat, photographed in 2005. Contemporary photo. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: On 15 June 1215 King John of England puts his seal to Magna Carta at Runnymede near Windsor, to make peace with rebellious barons. The charter limits the king's power, especially over taxes, and gives the barons a council of 25 members to see that it is followed. Pope Innocent III soon annuls it, and the First Barons' War breaks out. The charter is reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225, and three of the original clauses are still in force in England and Wales.

caption.en: Magna Carta from 1215, one of four surviving copies, in the British Library. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In the year 105 the official Cai Lun at the court in Luoyang presented the emperor with a new way of making paper. He boiled bark, hemp waste, old rags and fishing nets into a pulp that was mixed with water and strained into sheets. Paper became cheaper and soon replaced the heavy strips of bamboo and wood that people wrote on. Cai Lun has long been regarded as the inventor of paper, but archaeological finds show that paper existed in China even before the Common Era.

title.en: Was paper invented in the year 105?

text.en: The year 105 comes from Cai Lun's biography, which was written several hundred years later. The oldest surviving paper fragment was found at Fangmatan in Gansu and is dated to 179–141 BC; fragments have also been found at Dunhuang (65 BC) and the Yumen Pass (8 BC). Wikipedia's article on Cai Lun states that early forms of paper existed as early as the 3rd century BC. His contribution is therefore seen today as an improvement, not an invention. The place is the capital Luoyang, where he worked; today's city does not lie exactly where the Han-era capital stood.

summary.en: The Byzantine emperor Justinian I had Hagia Sophia built as the great church of Constantinople between 532 and 537. It replaced an older church on the same site that had been destroyed in the Nika riots. The building was designed by Isidore of Miletus and Anthemius of Tralles and had a dome over the largest interior space in the world at the time. It was the world's largest church for more than 500 years. After 1453 it became a mosque, later a museum and since 2020 a mosque again.

caption.en: Hagia Sophia in Istanbul. Modern photo (2013). Detail. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: Between 541 and 549 plague spread across the whole Mediterranean region, Europe and the Near East. The infection reached Egypt in 541 and was at its worst in the capital Constantinople, where about a fifth of the inhabitants died according to the historian Procopius. Emperor Justinian I himself fell ill but survived. Researchers have shown that the disease was caused by the same bacterium that later produced the Black Death. How great the consequences were is disputed among historians.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 541–549 for this first outbreak. Wikidata gives 541–750, which probably refers to the whole first plague pandemic with later waves.

summary.en: The House of Wisdom was a large library and centre of learning in Baghdad in the Abbasid era. It began in the 8th century, either as caliph al-Mansur's book collection or as Harun al-Rashid's library. Under the caliph al-Ma'mun (813–833) it became a public academy and a library. It was destroyed in 1258 when the Mongols besieged Baghdad. How large and well organised it was is debated by historians today.

The Tale of Genji was written by the court lady and poet Murasaki Shikibu in the early 11th century, at the height of the Heian period. It depicts life among the nobility at the imperial court and is about the emperor's son Genji and later his descendants. The book was written mostly in the Japanese syllabic script hiragana. It is often regarded as one of the world's first novels and has a standing in Japan similar to Shakespeare's in England. The original does not survive, but over 300 later copies do.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the book says the early 11th century and that it existed before about 1021. The article on Murasaki Shikibu gives about 1000–1012. Wikidata gives the 1010s. The oldest secure record of the book is from 1008.

caption.en: Fragment of a 12th-century picture scroll (emaki) of The Tale of Genji. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The Rapa Nui people of Easter Island in eastern Polynesia carved large stone statues, moai, roughly between 1250 and 1500. The statues represent divine ancestors and have very large heads. Almost half remain at the Rano Raraku quarry, but hundreds were transported around the island and erected on stone platforms. There are more than 900 statues, and the tallest erected one is almost 10 metres. All the statues had fallen over before the end of the 19th century.

caption.en: Moai at Ahu Tongariki. Modern photo (2006). Detail. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: In 541 the Byzantine historian Procopius reported an epidemic from the port city of Pelusium in Egypt. The infection, plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, then spread around the Mediterranean until 544 and persisted in northern Europe and on the Arabian Peninsula until 549. How many died is uncertain, and researchers disagree about how great the consequences were.

Around the year 670 the Umayyads founded the city of Kairouan, and the Arab general Uqba ibn Nafi is named as its founder. The city's Great Mosque was first built when the city was founded and is one of the oldest places of prayer in the Islamic world. Between the 9th and 11th centuries Kairouan was one of the great centres of learning in North Africa. Today the city is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez was founded as a mosque in the 9th century, when the city was the capital of the Idrisids. The mosque became one of the Islamic world's important centres of religion and education and was long run as a madrasa. UNESCO and Guinness World Records have called it the world's oldest university, but many scholars regard it as a university only from the reorganisation in 1963.

text.en: According to an early chronicle (Rawd al-Qirtas), the mosque was founded in 857 or 859 by Fatima al-Fihri, and Wikidata gives 859. A foundation inscription found in the 20th century says instead that Dawud ibn Idris founded the mosque in the year 877, and several scholars think the story of Fatima al-Fihri may be a legend.

summary.en: In 969 the Fatimid Caliphate conquered Egypt, and the caliph al-Muizz had the general Jawhar lay out a new fortified city north-east of Fustat. The construction took four years, and in 973 the city became the Fatimids' capital. The al-Azhar Mosque was built in 970–972 in the new city and in time developed into a seat of learning.

Around 1068 the scholar al-Bakri of Córdoba completed his book on roads and kingdoms, with a detailed description of the capital of the Ghana Empire. He described two towns on a plain, one for Muslim merchants with twelve mosques and one for the king. Al-Bakri never travelled there himself but relied on older texts and on people he met in Spain. The ruins at Koumbi Saleh have long been seen as this capital, but scholars increasingly question that.

According to an older Arabic tradition, the Almoravids under Abu Bakr ibn Umar conquered the Ghana Empire around 1076–77. Several modern scholars believe that no such military conquest ever took place, and archaeology shows no traces of rapid destruction. The country did, however, convert to Islam around 1076.

text.en: Ibn Khaldun, who wrote about 300 years later, relates that the Almoravids weakened Ghana. The scholars Conrad and Fisher (1982) call the conquest folklore based on misinterpreted Arabic sources, while others believe that there may nevertheless have been conflict or political influence. Whether war occurred is thus disputed.

summary.en: Around the year 1000, people of the Leopard's Kopje culture moved south to Bambandyanalo (K2) on the Limpopo, where they farmed, kept cattle and traded via the Swahili cities on the Indian Ocean. Around 1220, during a drought, the elite moved up onto Mapungubwe Hill. From there ivory and gold were exported to the east coast, and the capital had about 5,000 inhabitants around 1250. Around 1300 the population moved away. Today the site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

text.en: Wikipedia dates the kingdom of Mapungubwe from about 1220 to about 1300, with K2 (about 1000–1220) as its predecessor. Wikidata instead gives the kingdom as 1075–1220.

summary.en: In Lalibela in the Ethiopian highlands there are eleven churches carved out of a single piece of rock. According to tradition they were created under King Gebre Meskel Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty, who reigned about 1181–1221, and most reckon that they were built in the 12th and 13th centuries. According to a local tradition, the king was to build a second Jerusalem in Ethiopia. The churches are still used by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church and became a World Heritage Site in 1978.

text.en: How old the churches are is disputed. Wikipedia states that they are traditionally dated to the time of King Lalibela (about 1181–1221), but that they probably took shape in several building phases; one scholar believes the work continued into the 14th century, another that some of them were carved as early as 600–800. Wikidata gives the 13th century (century precision).

caption.en: Bete Giyorgis, one of the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela. Modern photo (2018). Detail. Licence: CC BY 3.0.

summary.en: In Ife, artists cast naturalistic heads in copper alloy, probably during the 14th or 15th century. One of them, the Ife Head, is thought to represent a king (ooni). It was found in 1938 during house building in Ife together with 16 other heads and is today in the British Museum. The finds upset Western notions of African civilisation.

When the first mosque in Djenné was built is unknown; scholars have proposed anything from about 1200 to 1330. According to the 17th-century chronicle Tarikh al-Sudan, the sultan Kunburu became a Muslim, had his palace torn down and made the site a mosque. The present mosque of sun-dried mud brick was rebuilt in 1906–1907 and is regarded as the world's largest mud-brick building.

caption.en: The Great Mosque of Djenné. Modern photo (2003). Detail. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: In the early 14th century Kilwa is the most powerful city on the Swahili Coast. The city trades gold, iron and ivory from the interior for beads, cloth, porcelain and spices from Asia. The sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman builds the palace Husuni Kubwa of coral stone and extends the Great Mosque with a large dome. The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta visited Kilwa in 1331 and described the city as one of the most beautiful in the world.

Around 1390 the Kingdom of Kongo in Central Africa is founded through a political marriage between Nimi a Nzima, ruler of Mpemba Kasi and Vungu, and Lukeni lua Nsanze, daughter of the ruler of the neighbouring kingdom of Mbata. Their son Lukeni lua Nimi extends the kingdom southwards and becomes its first king. The capital became Mbanza Kongo, later called São Salvador. Kongo was an independent kingdom for almost 500 years.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the kingdom was founded around 1390, while Wikidata gives 1395. The place matches.

summary.en: The Portuguese navigator Bartolomeu Dias leaves Lisbon with three ships around July 1487. After 30 days on the open sea he reaches, on 4 February 1488, the south coast of Africa at what is later called Mossel Bay, and becomes the first European to sail around the southern tip of Africa. On the way home in May 1488 he sees the Cape of Good Hope. Portugal had thereby reached its long-sought goal. No contemporary documents about the voyage have been found.

Around AD 200 the Pyramid of the Sun, the largest building in Teotihuacan, was built almost to the size it has today. During the first centuries AD Teotihuacan grew into Mesoamerica's largest city, and around AD 450, 150,000 people may have lived there. The name Teotihuacan was given by the Aztecs long after the city fell around AD 550.

caption.en: The Avenue of the Dead and the Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacán. Modern photo (2020). Detail. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: Between roughly the year 1 and 400, the Hopewell culture built large earthworks in geometric shapes along tributaries of the Ohio River. At the Octagon Earthworks in Newark, three-metre-high earth walls surround an octagon, probably built in alignment with the movements of the sun and moon. Eight of the sites became World Heritage Sites in 2023.

The Moche culture flourished in northern Peru from about AD 100 to 800 and is known for its ceramics and its adobe pyramids. In 1987 the archaeologist Walter Alva found an intact royal tomb at Huaca Rajada near Sipán. The dead man, called the Lord of Sipán, was 35–45 years old and was buried with jewellery of gold and silver and six other people. By 2007 fourteen tombs had been found at the site.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the Moche culture flourished about AD 100–800, while Wikidata gives about the years 1–700. Wikipedia dates Sipán to AD 50–700.

summary.en: Kʼinich Janaabʼ Pakal, also called Pakal the Great, ruled the Maya city of Palenque from 615 until his death in 683, for 68 years. He extended Palenque's power among the western Maya states and had some of the Maya culture's finest works of art and architecture erected, including a major extension of the palace. He was buried in the Temple of the Inscriptions, Palenque's largest step pyramid, which was built as his funerary monument and completed shortly after 683 by his son. The tomb was not discovered until 1952.

Tiwanaku in western Bolivia, near Lake Titicaca, is one of South America's largest archaeological sites. The city grew during the first centuries of the Common Era and became significant roughly 375–700; at its height it covered about 4 square kilometres and had more than 10,000 inhabitants. The Tiwanaku culture was at its strongest around 500–600. The society collapsed around the year 1000, and drought in the region probably played a part.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the society collapsed around the year 1000 (the fact box says that the site was abandoned around 1050), while Wikidata gives the period 400–900.

caption.en: The Gateway of the Sun at Tiwanaku. Modern photo. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The Wari Empire emerged around the year 600 in the Ayacucho Basin in Peru and came to cover large parts of Peru's coast and highlands. The capital was Huari, and the provincial cities were linked to the capital by a network of roads. The oldest known quipus, knotted cords used in the Andes for keeping records, are attributed to the Wari. The empire came to an end during the 11th century.

Between about 900 and 1150, Chaco Canyon was a major cultural centre for the Ancestral Puebloans. They quarried sandstone and hauled timber long distances to build 15 large complexes, so-called great houses, which remained the largest buildings in North America until the 19th century. The largest, Pueblo Bonito, had at least 650 rooms and was four storeys high in places. A 50-year drought that began in 1130 is thought to have contributed to the abandonment of the canyon.

Cahokia was a city that existed roughly 1050–1350 and the largest and most influential city of the Mississippian culture. Its population is estimated at between 6,000 and 40,000 at its largest. The city had up to 120 earthen mounds; the largest, Monks Mound, is about 30 metres high and the largest artificial earthen mound north of Mexico. From about 1160–1170 the population began to decline, and the city was abandoned around 1400.

Chichén Itzá in the state of Yucatán was one of the largest cities of the Maya culture. The core of the city was laid out around 750–900, and between 900 and 1050 it grew into a mighty regional capital that ruled northern and central Yucatán. The best-known structure is the Temple of Kukulcán, which the Spaniards called El Castillo. According to archaeological finds, the city had lost its role as a regional centre around 1100.

text.en: Wikipedia states that Chichén Itzá was founded around 750 and lost its standing around 1100 (the site was abandoned during the 13th century), while Wikidata gives the founding as 455 and the end as 1178.

caption.en: El Castillo (the Pyramid of Kukulcán) at Chichén Itzá. Modern photo (2009). Detail. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: Chan Chan was built, according to researchers, around 850 by the Chimú people in Peru's dry coastal desert and became the capital of the Chimor Empire, with an estimated 40,000–60,000 inhabitants. The ruins cover about 20 square kilometres, and Chan Chan is regarded as the largest mud-brick (adobe) city in the Americas. After the Inca conquered the Chimú around 1470, the city fell into decline.

caption.en: Chan Chan. Modern photo (2023). Detail. Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0.

summary.en: Towards the end of the 12th century the Ancestral Puebloans at Mesa Verde began to build large dwellings in alcoves along the canyon walls. The largest, Cliff Palace, is North America's largest cliff dwelling; it was built and inhabited roughly 1200–1300 and has 21 kivas, round sunken rooms for ceremonies. After a severe drought the last inhabitants left the area around 1285 and moved south to today's Arizona and New Mexico.

caption.en: Cliff Palace at Mesa Verde. Photograph by Gustaf Nordenskiöld from 1891. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: When the Tepanec king Tezozomoc died in 1426, a struggle for power broke out. In 1427 Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, Tlacopan and Huexotzinco went to war against the Tepanec city of Azcapotzalco and won in 1428. In 1430 Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan concluded a treaty, today called the Triple Alliance, and divided the Tepanec land among themselves. The alliance, which is also called the Aztec Empire, ruled the Valley of Mexico until the Spanish conquest in 1521, and Tenochtitlan in time became the dominant city.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 1428 as the start of the alliance's rule but 1430 for the treaty itself. Wikidata gives for the Aztec Empire the founding as 1325 and the start as 1367.

summary.en: Pachacuti was the ninth Inca ruler in Cusco and transformed the chiefdom of Cusco into the Inca Empire, Tawantinsuyu. He came to power after the war against the Chanka people and conquered, among other things, land around Lake Titicaca and northwards towards Quito, which began the Inca expansion in the Andes. Most archaeologists believe that Machu Picchu was built as an estate for him. The Inca did not count years in a systematic way, so his reign is uncertain: the usual chronology says 1438–1471.

text.en: Researchers give different reigns: 1438–1471 (Rowe, the usual chronology), 1425–1471 (del Busto), 1400–1448 (Means) and 1410–1450 (Jaguaribe); carbon-14 dating points to the early 15th century. Wikidata gives the year of death as 1460 or 1471.

summary.en: The history of Hawaii begins when Polynesians come to the Hawaiian Islands. When this happened is disputed. The latest review of carbon-14 dates puts the arrival at about 940–1130, while older assessments have given anything from about the year 300 to 700–800. The Polynesians' history was handed down through genealogical chants recited at festivals.

text.en: Wikipedia reports several datings: Patrick Kirch's textbooks give about the year 300 and later about 600, other theories 700–800, and the latest review of carbon-14 dates about 940–1130. The introduction of the same article gives 940–1200.

summary.en: Polynesians reach Rapa Nui, the far south-east of the Polynesian Triangle, probably in the 12th century according to the best assessment today. They probably came by canoe or catamaran from Mangareva, about 2,600 km away, or the Marquesas Islands, about 3,200 km away. According to oral tradition the first settlers were led by the chief Hotu Matuʻa. Between about 1250 and 1500 the Rapa Nui people carved moai, over 900 large stone statues, most of them from tuff from the Rano Raraku quarry.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the datings of the first settlement have varied from the year 400 to 1300. Many researchers have pointed to about the year 800, while a study from 2007 argues for closer to 1200; the best assessment today is the 12th century.

summary.en: Around the year 950 the first Tuʻi Tonga, King ʻAhoʻeitu, begins to extend his rule beyond Tonga. The empire had its centre on the island of Tongatapu with the capital Muʻa and was at its largest around 1200–1500. Every year after the harvest, gifts were brought to the Tuʻi Tonga in Muʻa from the areas under his authority. Research confirms a broad Tongan influence, including on Samoa, Niue, Wallis and Futuna.

In the 13th century Haʻamonga ʻa Maui is built, a gateway of three large blocks of coral limestone, 5.2 metres high. According to historical analysis, Tuʻitātui, the eleventh Tuʻi Tonga, had it built around the year 1200 in memory of his two sons, probably as the entrance to the royal area of Heketā. Each standing stone visibly weighs about 30–40 tonnes. The monument is sometimes called the Stonehenge of the Pacific.

caption.en: Haʻamonga ʻa Maui on Tonga. Modern photo (2008). Detail. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: Around 1180–1200 construction begins on the megalithic city of Nan Madol on Pohnpei's east coast, with large basalt blocks brought from the other side of the island. The city consists of 92 artificial islands in a lagoon, separated by canals. It was the seat of the Saudeleur dynasty, the first government to unite Pohnpei's estimated 25,000 inhabitants, until about 1628, when Isokelekel overthrew it.

caption.en: Nan Madol. Modern photo. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: At Wairau Bar, a gravel bar where the Wairau River meets the sea, explorers from eastern Polynesia settled. Carbon-14 dating gives the settlement the years 1288–1300, and it was used twice over about 20 years. The graves contained, among other things, necklaces of moa bone and whole moa eggs. DNA analyses show that the oldest graves belong to people who had lived in eastern Polynesia.

Polynesians from mainland New Zealand come to the Chatham Islands, Rēkohu, by about 1500 at the latest and perhaps around the middle of the 15th century; some may have come earlier directly from eastern Polynesia. There the Moriori emerge as a people of their own with their own language, mythology and art. In the 16th century the leader Nunuku-whenua forbade war and cannibalism, and disputes were instead settled with ritual combat and reconciliation.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the arrival took place by about 1500 at the latest, the oldest carbon-14-dated trace, and perhaps around 1450, but that older objects suggest it was earlier. The New Zealand Moriori Claims Settlement Act, which Wikipedia links to, gives 1000–1400.

summary.en: Marae Taputapuātea at Opoa on Raiatea may have been laid out as early as around the year 1000 and was rebuilt and extended at least twice between the 14th and 18th centuries. The site was once regarded as the central temple of eastern Polynesia. First the creator god Taʻaroa was worshipped there, later the god ʻOro. Priests and navigators from all over the Pacific gathered there to make offerings and share knowledge of ocean navigation. Since 2017 the site has been a World Heritage Site.

Around the year 900 the Chamorro people of the Mariana Islands begin to use latte stones, pillars with a hemispherical capstone, as supports for buildings. They became increasingly common until Ferdinand Magellan arrived in 1521 and the Spaniards colonised the islands, and by about 1700 they had been abandoned entirely. The largest one still standing is 5 metres high and is on Tinian. In Oceania latte stones exist only in the Mariana Islands, and today they are a symbol of Chamorro identity.

In the 4th century large stone stelae were carved and erected in Aksum. They were probably markers for underground burial chambers, and the largest, for royal tombs, have false doors and windows. King Ezana's Stele is 21 metres high and still stands, the so-called Obelisk of Aksum is 24 metres, and the largest, 33 metres, lies fallen. The custom was abandoned after Aksum became Christian under King Ezana.

The Kanem Empire, the beginning of what is called Kanem-Bornu, is usually dated to about the year 700. The core was the region of Kanem north-east of Lake Chad, and the capital Njimi has never been found. The empire lived on trans-Saharan trade and converted to Islam in the 11th century. Around 1380 the Bilala people took Kanem and Njimi, and the centre of the empire moved to Bornu west of the lake.

text.en: Wikipedia says that the empire is most often dated to about 700, but that some scholars give about 600 or about 900. Wikidata gives the 11th century as the start of Kanem-Bornu.

summary.en: Marrakesh was founded by Abu Bakr ibn Umar as the capital of the Almoravid dynasty, according to most modern historians around 1070. The Almoravids built the city's first mosques and a fortified palace, and the square Jemaa el-Fnaa grew out of the space in front of the palace gates. The city quickly became a centre of trade, culture and religion in the Maghreb.

text.en: Historical sources give years between 1062 (Ibn Abi Zar and Ibn Khaldun) and 1078 (al-Idrisi). Modern historians most often use 1070, but 1062 also occurs. Wikidata gives 1065.

summary.en: In 1270 Yekuno Amlak, a ruler from Bete Amhara, overthrew the last king of the Zagwe dynasty and became emperor of Ethiopia. He founded the Solomonic dynasty, which held power until 1974. Later writings claimed that he descended from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba via the royal house of Aksum, but historians see the story as legends meant to make the seizure of power legitimate.

Ewuare was oba, or king, of Benin from about 1440 to 1473. He became king through a violent coup against his brother, and the fighting destroyed large parts of Benin City. He then rebuilt the capital with walls, moats and broad streets, strengthened royal power and greatly expanded the kingdom. He is often regarded as the first king of the Kingdom of Benin.

Cuicuilco on the southern shore of Lake Texcoco may be the oldest city in the Valley of Mexico, and its pyramid began to be built a few centuries before the Common Era. At its height the city had about 20,000 inhabitants, but it declined as Teotihuacan grew. It was destroyed and abandoned after an eruption of the volcano Xitle, and the lava covered large parts of the city. Refugees are thought to have moved north and become part of Teotihuacan's population.

text.en: The time of the eruption is given differently: between 245 and 315 AD, about 400 AD, with the city abandoned about 150–200 AD, and according to some sources already during the 1st century BC. Here the span 245–315 is shown.

summary.en: Quiriguá was a small vassal state under the powerful Maya city of Copán. In 738, Quiriguá's king K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat took Copán's king Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil captive, and on 3 May 738 he was beheaded in a public ceremony at Quiriguá. There are no traces of either city having been attacked; Quiriguá became independent and gained control of important trade routes. Calakmul may have played a part behind the coup. In Copán, no new buildings or monuments were erected for 18 years afterwards.

Tula, in today's state of Hidalgo, became important after the fall of Teotihuacan and was at its largest between about 900 and 1150. The city then covered about 14 square kilometres with around 60,000 inhabitants. It lived on agriculture and on mining and working obsidian. Best known is the Pyramid of Quetzalcoatl, where four four-metre-tall basalt warrior figures held up the roof of the temple. Drought and ethnic conflicts contributed to the city's fall around 1150, but Tula lived on in Aztec history, which is often mixed with myth.

Eight Deer Jaguar Claw was born in Tilantongo in 1063 and became a powerful Mixtec ruler in Oaxaca. Most of what we know about him comes from pictorial manuscripts, chiefly the Codex Zouche-Nuttall, which lists 94 cities conquered in his time. He was the only Mixtec king to unite the kingdoms in all three Mixtec regions: Tilantongo, Teozacoalco and Tututepec. He died in 1115, but the accounts of his death differ, and the interpretation of the manuscripts is still uncertain.

The Thule people, ancestors of today's Inuit and Yupik, developed in the coastal lands of Alaska around the year 1000. With dog sleds, umiaks and kayaks they spread east across northern Canada and reached Greenland by the 13th century at the latest. On the way they replaced the older Dorset culture. The name comes from Thule, today Pituffik in northwest Greenland, where remains of the people were first found.

In 1493 the general Muhammad Ture defeated the new ruler Sunni Baru and became king of the Songhai Empire, Askia Muhammad. Under him the empire became the largest in West African history. He built up an administration, standard measures for trade and a tax system, and made Islam an important part of the empire. He ruled until 1528, when his son Askia Musa overthrew him.

Paquimé, also called Casas Grandes, is an archaeological site in northern Mexico attributed to the Mogollon culture. The settlement began after 1130, and after 1350 the large buildings grew into multi-storey houses. Farming relied on irrigation. The site was abandoned around 1450 and is today a World Heritage Site.

In the 15th century, the landmass of Kuwae near the island of Tongoa was destroyed by a large volcanic eruption, probably when the volcano collapsed into a caldera. Glowing ash clouds covered large parts of Tongoa and Epi. According to stories on Tongoa, the young Ti Tongoa Liseiriki survived and was the first to move back. Where the eruption was located and how large it was is still disputed.

text.en: The eruption was first linked to a sulphur peak in the ice of Antarctica, dated to about 1452–1453. A 2012 study redated the peak to 1458, and it is not certain that it comes from Kuwae. Carbon-14 on Ti Tongoa Liseiriki's bones gives 1475 ± 85 years. Wikidata gives no year.

summary.en: Around 1314, with an uncertainty of about 12 years, the volcano Tarawera had a large explosive eruption, the Kaharoa eruption. It took place in several phases from a long fissure, and the ash spread over large parts of the North Island. It happened shortly after the first Māori had arrived in New Zealand, around 1280.

Rangitoto, the youngest and largest of about 50 volcanoes in the Auckland volcanic field, formed about 600 years ago in two phases that may have lasted only 5–10 years. The eruptions produced almost as much material as all earlier eruptions in the volcanic field over nearly 200,000 years. The Māori witnessed the eruption, and footprints have been found between the ash layers on the neighbouring island of Motutapu.

text.en: Wikipedia states in its introduction that the eruptions took place around 1450 and 1500, but the radiocarbon datings in the same article (553 ± 7 and 504 ± 5 years before 1950) correspond to around 1400 and 1450. Wikidata gives no year.

summary.en: The moa were flightless giant birds found only in New Zealand. After Polynesians came to the islands, some time before 1300, all species died out, mainly because of hunting but also because forest was cleared, and by about 1445 none were left; datings of refuse heaps suggest that it took less than a hundred years. At the same time Haast's eagle, the largest eagle known, which had lived on moa, went extinct.

text.en: Wikipedia states that all moa were extinct by about 1445. Wikidata gives 1500 as the end year for the moa.

summary.en: Pulemelei is the largest and oldest structure built by people in the Samoan Islands: a pyramid-like mound of basalt stone in several terraces, aligned with the cardinal directions. Excavations in 2002–2004 show that it was probably built between 1100 and 1400 and went out of use around 1700–1800. It is interpreted as an important ceremonial site in a society with chiefs.

Around 1470 the royal dynasty Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua was founded by Moʻungāmotuʻa, who may at first have been a deputy king under his brother, the Tuʻi Tonga. He gradually took over political power and sent his brother into exile in Samoa, but let the title of Tuʻi Tonga remain. The Tuʻi Tonga then became mainly a spiritual leader in Muʻa.

Traces of a Polynesian settlement, perhaps from the 13th century, have been found on Enderby Island in the subantarctic Auckland Islands. It is the southernmost Polynesian settlement known. Polynesian seafarers were thus the first to discover the islands.

Archaeological finds suggest that Norfolk Island was settled in the 13th or 14th century by East Polynesian seafarers, either from the Kermadec Islands or from New Zealand's North Island. Melanesian objects have also been found, so people from New Caledonia may also have come there. When the British arrived in 1788 the island was uninhabited.

Settlement sites on northern Raoul Island, the largest of the Kermadec Islands, show that Polynesians lived there in the 14th century. Obsidian of the same kind has been found at early Māori settlements on New Zealand's South Island. Researchers believe the island was a short-lived stepping stone on the voyages between Polynesia and New Zealand.

Polynesians settled on Henderson Island, perhaps as early as around the year 800, and on the neighbouring island of Pitcairn. The small islands depended on Mangareva and Pitcairn, for example for stone for tools. When Mangareva declined, Henderson was abandoned first and Pitcairn later, and the reason the inhabitants disappeared is still uncertain.

text.en: The article on Henderson Island says the island was abandoned in the 17th century, while the article on the Pitcairn Islands says Henderson was probably abandoned before the 16th century and Pitcairn in the 17th or early 18th century. Wikidata gives no years.

summary.en: Mangareva was settled by Polynesians during the first millennium, probably around the year 800. The island was forested and had a large population that traded with other islands by canoe. Between the 10th century and the 15th century the forest was cut down, which had severe consequences for both nature and trade.

text.en: The article on Mangareva gives about 800, but carbon-14 has so far only yielded settlement sites from 1160–1220, and traces of trade exist from about 1000. The article on the Gambier Islands considers it more likely that the islands were settled from the Society Islands around the year 1000.

summary.en: The Marquesas Islands were settled by Polynesians from western Polynesia, descendants of the Lapita culture. A 2010 study with more precise carbon-14 datings shows that eastern Polynesia was settled late and quickly: first the Society Islands around 1025–1120 and then, in a second wave, the Marquesas Islands around 1190–1290.

text.en: Wikipedia also mentions that archaeological research points to the 10th century, and that older datings have given before the year 100 or around 600. Here the 2010 study is used. Wikidata gives no year.

summary.en: The first Polynesians came to the Society Islands, where Tahiti is the largest island, around the year 1000. According to a 2010 study it happened between about 1025 and 1120, several hundred years later than previously thought. From here the settlement of eastern Polynesia continued.

In the later part of the 15th century the chief Piʻilani became the first to bring the whole island of Maui under a single lineage. According to tradition his rule was mostly peaceful. He began building a road around the whole island, the first of its kind in the Hawaiian Islands, which his son completed.

Roi Mata was a chiefly title in central Vanuatu borne by a long line of chiefs from the 11th century to the 17th century. The best known was the last, who is thought to have lived around the year 1600. His grave on the island of Eretoka, with the bodies of more than 25 people from his retinue, was found in 1967 with the help of local stories and became a World Heritage Site in 2008.

In 930 the Icelanders gathered for the first time at the Althing, an open-air assembly on the plain of Þingvellir east of today's Reykjavík. It is regarded as the world's oldest legislative assembly. At the Law Rock (Lögberg) the Lawspeaker sat and presided over the assembly. After Iceland came under the King of Norway in 1262, the Althing lost its legislative power.

In 862 the Byzantine emperor sent the brothers Cyril and Methodius from Thessalonica as missionaries to Great Moravia, at the request of Prince Rastislav. Cyril created the Glagolitic alphabet, the oldest known Slavic alphabet, to translate Greek church texts into Old Church Slavonic. It was used in Great Moravia from 863. Later the Cyrillic alphabet emerged in Bulgaria and gradually took over there.

Around the year 988, Prince Vladimir the Great was baptised at Chersonesos in Crimea and then had his family and his people baptised in Kiev. The event is known as the Baptism of Rus'. Christianity had, however, begun to spread in Rus' earlier, and the conversion was a long process. The year is disputed.

caption.en: The Christianization of Kievan Rus’ in a painting by Klavdy Lebedev (before 1916), not a contemporary image. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: In 785 Abd al-Rahman I, founder of the Emirate of Córdoba, had a large mosque begun. Construction went quickly, partly thanks to reused Roman and Visigothic columns, and was finished in 786–787. The mosque was extended several times until the end of the 10th century. When Castile conquered Córdoba in 1236 it was converted into a cathedral.

caption.en: The Mosque of Córdoba seen from the air. Modern photo (2010). Detail. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

summary.en: The Hanseatic League was a loose association of trading towns that grew up around Lübeck and other north German towns from the end of the 12th century. It never had a formal founding, but historians have often counted from 1159, when Lübeck was rebuilt. At its largest the League comprised almost 200 places from Estonia and Russia to the Netherlands, with offices in, among others, London, Bruges, Bergen and Novgorod. It was dissolved in 1669.

text.en: Wikipedia says the Hanseatic League has no founding year and mentions 1159 as the traditional starting point, with dissolution in 1669. Wikidata gives 1358 as the beginning and 1862 as the end.

summary.en: Around the year 232, with an uncertainty of about ten years, the Taupō volcano had its most recent major eruption. It is regarded as New Zealand's largest eruption in the past 20,000 years. A pyroclastic flow moved at nearly the speed of sound and covered the ground within 80 km with ignimbrite, and Lake Taupō became larger. No people yet lived in New Zealand; the Māori came more than 1,000 years later.

text.en: Wikipedia gives the year 232 ± 10, within a wider span of 205–373 from palaeomagnetic dating, and writes that the age is still somewhat disputed. Wikidata gives the year 180.
